newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll in Dreux is new test for French far-right.
newsitem.headline: Poll in Dreux is new test for French far-right.

text.p: Voters in Dreux, central France, cast their ballots on Sunday in a municipal poll widely seen as a key test for the governing centre-right, which faces strong challenges from both the left and the far-right National Front.

The city hall in Dreux, about 80 km (50 miles) west of Paris, is currently in the hands of the centre-right but the city is best known as the scene of one of the first electoral breakthroughs by the virulently anti-immigration National Front.
The Front scored so well in a 1983 city poll that local officials of the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR), the senior partner in the current governing coalition, offered it an alliance.
The resulting electoral pact scandalised the left and was also denounced by national party leaders including now-president Jacques Chirac.

But the right's appeal in Dreux remains so strong that the opposition Socialists have been excluded from local,power for a generation, failing even to qualify for a run-off in the last 23 years of municipal voting.
With the national government plumbing record lows in approval ratings and unemployment at a record 12.6 percent, the Socialists say 1996 may finally be their lucky year.
But the National Front, whose fiery leader Jean-Marie Le Pen won 15 percent of the vote in 1995 presidential elections, was also feeling optimistic as the Dreux poll got under way.
Its slate led by European Parliamentarian Marie-France Stirbois won 39 percent of the vote in the run-off round of 1995 municipal elections.

Since then, with voters concerned by soaring urban crime and unemployment, the Front has been climbing in public opinion polls across France. The party's ratings rose even after Le Pen said recently he believed in racial inequality, triggering a firestorm of protest from mainstream politicians.
The RPR won the 1995 poll in Dreux with 61 percent of the second-round vote, making Gaullist Gerard Hamel the mayor. The Front's 39 percent won it seven of the city council's 39 seats.
But the state council, France's highest constitutional authority, later ordered Hamel's election invalidated over a conflict of interest.
In a show of solidarity, the entire centre-right slate resigned, forcing a new election.

Socialist Party chief Lionel Jospin gave a boost last week to the combined leftist slate, led by Socialist Maurice Ravanne, visiting Dreux to urge that Sunday's poll be made a referendum on national government policies.
Le Pen, also visiting the city last week, made a similar appeal.
Hamel, on the other hand, sought to frame the vote as a referendum on his accomplishments as mayor to date and his unfinished agenda. REUTER
